The Common spotted cuscus (Spilocuscus maculatus) exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its arboreal, folivorous-frugivorous lifestyle within the lowland rainforests of New Guinea and adjacent islands. In terms of neonatal development, newborn offspring enter the world at a remarkably modest size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.9 grams [Wwb = 0.9 grams]. This altricial neonate is utterly dependent on maternal care immediately following parturition, a typical pattern for marsupials where the tiny joey must crawl to the pouch to commence its protracted period of postnatal development. The energetic costs of gestation itself are relatively brief; the gestation time has been recorded as 13 days [tg = 13 days] when measured at a standard ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This exceptionally short intrauterine period is characteristic of marsupials, where the majority of growth and differentiation occurs postnatally within the protective environment of the pouch, rather than during a prolonged placental gestation.

Following the neonatal period, the suckling juvenile undergoes a prolonged phase of dependency within the maternal pouch and later as a back-riding young. The transition to nutritional independence, or weaning, does not occur until the offspring has reached a substantial wet weight at weaning of 1700 grams [Wwx = 1700 grams]. This milestone is attained after a significant developmental interval; the time since birth at weaning is approximately 240 days [tx = approximately 240 days] under the thermal conditions typical of their tropical habitat, specifically when ambient temperature is maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This extended suckling period allows for the gradual development of complex motor skills necessary for navigating the three-dimensional forest canopy and for the maturation of digestive physiology required to process a diet of leaves and fruits. The substantial body mass achieved by the time the mother ceases provisioning is critical for the juvenile's subsequent survival and growth into the independent juvenile stage.

The onset of reproductive capability in Spilocuscus maculatus is sexually dimorphic, reflecting different selective pressures on males and females regarding territory acquisition and mate competition. Data collected under controlled captive conditions, with subjects held at a stable 35 °C [T = 35 °C], indicate that females attain puberty, as defined by the time since birth at puberty, at 222 days [tp = 222 days]. This signal of reproductive activation marks the point at which a female is physiologically capable of ovulation and conception, though first breeding may be deferred by social or ecological constraints. Males, in contrast, reach puberty somewhat later; the corresponding time since birth at puberty for males is 243 days [tp = 243 days], measured under identical temperature conditions. This disparity is commonly observed in polygynous or promiscuous mammalian systems where male reproductive success hinges on body size and competitive ability.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by its slow-paced life history and the energetic demands of lactation. While a theoretical maximum may exist, field records and captive breeding data indicate that females generally produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year]. Defining this reproductive rate more precisely under the stable thermal conditions of the laboratory, taken to be 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the maximum frequency of reproduction equates to a single annual event. This low fecundity is balanced by a relatively high investment per offspring, evidenced by the considerable mass at weaning and the extended period of maternal care. Such a reproductive strategy is typical of mammals inhabiting stable tropical environments where high adult survival and intense sibling competition select for quality over quantity.

The metabolic underpinnings of this leisurely life-history pace are quantified by measurements of basal oxygen consumption. Respirometry trials conducted at a thermoneutral temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] reveal that the maximum basal metabolic rate for this species is approximately 1020 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 1020 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. Considering the species' ultimate wet weight, which can reach up to 5000 grams [Wwi = up to 5000 grams] in large adult males, this represents a relatively modest mass-specific metabolic rate compared to eutherian mammals of similar mass. This reduced expenditure aligns with an extended lifespan; the maximum recorded longevity for Spilocuscus maculatus in captivity, under the same thermal regime of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], is 6205 days [am = 6205 days]. This combination of a low metabolic rate, a late age at maturity, and a slow reproductive rate is a classic signature of a "slow" life-history strategy, an adaptation to the relatively predictable and resource-dispersed nature of its rainforest habitat.
